The finding is a closed-period posting: journal 2463 was posted on 20240808 into period 7, which closed on 20240805. The posted rows cannot be edited, and nothing in the evidence shows the amounts or accounts are wrong. The problem is only the period it was booked in.

The usual fix is to reverse the original journal's effect and re-book it in an open period, which gives a net-zero effect on the closed period's cumulative position. A correcting journal can only post to an open period (11 or 12), so the reversal and the re-booking both land in the same open period. Their combined effect on the account balances is nil, and the original stays in period 7.

I kept the correction as small as the finding allows by posting the lines in period 11, the earliest open period.

**Option A, reverse and re-book (a net-zero journal).** This only adds noise and moves nothing, so I decided against it.

**Option B, reverse the original in the open period.** Reversing the entry in period 11 would remove the accrual from the ledger altogether. That is only right if the entry should not exist, and the evidence does not show that. The accrual itself looks legitimate; the posting date is the only defect.

**Option C, move the effect to the open period.** The true position is that the expense and accruals are recognised in an open period instead of the closed one. Moving them means reversing the original lines in period 11 and re-booking the same lines in period 11. The combined effect of the original and my lines is then the original amounts, and the period-7 lines remain as posted history.

I went with option C. The correcting lines for 2463 are a reversal in period 11 (credit 5100 by 5382.28, debit 2100 and 1200 by 2691.14 each) plus a re-booking in period 11 (debit 5100 by 5382.28, credit 2100 and 1200 by 2691.14 each). Combined with the original journal, the net position is unchanged, the group balances, and the correction posts only to an open period. No invoice status changes, since this is not a duplicate invoice finding.
